heic.name: HEIC
heic.summary: HEIC is the HEIF container holding HEVC (H.265) compressed images. Apple made it the default camera format with iOS 11 in 2017 because it stores a photo in roughly half the space of a comparable JPEG, and it can carry 10-bit color, depth maps, alpha and image sequences such as Live Photo stills. The catch is compatibility: HEVC is patent-encumbered, so most browsers (other than Safari 17+), many Windows installs, older Android devices and countless upload forms cannot open it.

traits.transparency: Supported by the format; rare in camera photos
traits.colorDepth: 8 or 10 bits per channel, wide-gamut Display P3
traits.support: Safari 17+, Apple devices; Windows needs extra codecs; Chrome and Firefox cannot display it
traits.bestFor: Storing phone photos compactly inside the Apple ecosystem

avif.name: AVIF
avif.summary: AVIF stores still images and animations compressed with the royalty-free AV1 video codec inside a HEIF container. Published by the Alliance for Open Media in 2019, it typically beats both JPEG and WebP on file size at equal visual quality, supports alpha, HDR and 10/12-bit color, and is increasingly served by image CDNs. Modern browsers display it, but plenty of desktop software, email clients, office suites and upload forms still reject .avif files.

traits.compression: Lossy or lossless AV1 intra-frame coding
traits.colorDepth: 8, 10 or 12 bits per channel; HDR capable
traits.support: Chrome 85+, Firefox 93+, Safari 16.4+; patchy in desktop apps and upload forms
traits.bestFor: Web delivery where the smallest file wins

webp.name: WebP
webp.summary: WebP is Google's 2010 web image format based on VP8 intra-frame coding, later extended with a separate lossless mode, alpha and animation. Google's own comparison found lossy WebP files 25–34% smaller than JPEGs at equivalent SSIM quality. Every current browser supports it, which is why many websites now serve WebP automatically — and why people end up with .webp downloads that older photo editors, office documents and some print services will not accept.

traits.transparency: Full alpha channel in both modes
traits.colorDepth: 8 bits per channel, 4:2:0 chroma in lossy mode
traits.support: All current browsers; mixed in older desktop software
traits.bestFor: Web pages that need smaller images than JPEG or PNG

jpg.name: JPG
jpg.summary: JPEG, standardised in 1992, compresses photographs by discarding detail the eye is less sensitive to (via the discrete cosine transform on 8×8 blocks). It has no transparency and no animation, and every re-save loses a little more quality, but it is the most compatible image format in existence: every camera, phone, browser, operating system, office suite, printer and upload form accepts it.

traits.compression: Lossy DCT; quality chosen at save time
traits.support: Universal
traits.bestFor: Photos that must open anywhere

png.name: PNG
png.summary: PNG was created in 1996 as a patent-free replacement for GIF. It is lossless — pixels decode exactly as they were saved — and supports a full alpha channel, which makes it the default for screenshots, logos, UI graphics and anything with sharp edges or text. The trade-off is size: a photograph saved as PNG is often several times larger than the same photo as a JPEG.

traits.compression: Lossless DEFLATE with per-row prediction filters
traits.support: Universal
traits.bestFor: Screenshots, logos, graphics with transparency or text

svg.name: SVG
svg.summary: SVG is an XML-based W3C format that describes shapes, paths, gradients and text instead of pixels, so it stays sharp at any size. That makes it ideal for logos and icons on the web — but many places that accept images (social networks, marketplaces, office apps, email) reject SVG, partly because an SVG file can contain scripts and external references. Rasterising to PNG or JPG produces a fixed-size image those places accept.

traits.transparency: Yes — anything not drawn is transparent
traits.animation: Via SMIL or CSS (not preserved when rasterised)
traits.support: All browsers; limited in office apps, social platforms and many upload forms
traits.bestFor: Logos, icons and illustrations that must scale

gif.name: GIF
gif.summary: GIF dates from 1987 (CompuServe). Each frame is limited to a palette of at most 256 colors and compressed losslessly with LZW. Its support for multiple frames is why it became the internet's format for short looping animations, and it supports single-color (on/off) transparency. For still images it is almost always a poor choice today: colors get dithered and files are larger than PNG.

traits.compression: Lossless LZW, but limited to 256 colors per frame
traits.transparency: 1-bit (a pixel is fully transparent or fully opaque)
traits.animation: Supported — the format's main use today
traits.support: Universal
traits.bestFor: Short, simple looping animations

bmp.name: BMP
bmp.summary: BMP is the native bitmap format of Windows, dating back to Windows 1.0/OS2. Files are usually stored uncompressed, row by row (often bottom-up), which makes them simple to read but enormous: a 12-megapixel photo is about 36 MB as a 24-bit BMP. BMPs still come out of older scanners, screenshot tools, industrial equipment and legacy software.

traits.compression: Usually none; optional RLE for palette images
traits.support: Windows and all browsers; rejected by many upload forms because of size
traits.bestFor: Legacy software and raw pixel interchange

tiff.name: TIFF
tiff.summary: TIFF, created by Aldus in 1986 and now maintained by Adobe, is a flexible container used in scanning, print production, faxing, archiving and GIS. A single file can hold several pages and use one of many compression schemes (none, LZW, Deflate, PackBits, CCITT fax, JPEG). That flexibility is also its weakness: no browser except Safari displays TIFF, and most web forms refuse it.

traits.compression: None, LZW, Deflate, PackBits, CCITT or JPEG
traits.animation: No, but multiple pages per file
traits.colorDepth: 1 to 32 bits per channel, RGB, CMYK or grayscale
traits.support: Image editors and print tools; only Safari among browsers
traits.bestFor: Scans, print masters and archival images

ico.name: ICO
ico.summary: ICO is the Windows icon container, also the classic favicon.ico format for websites. One .ico file bundles several versions of the same icon at different sizes (commonly 16, 32, 48 and 256 pixels), each stored as either a PNG or an uncompressed BMP-style bitmap with an optional transparency mask. Most image editors and design tools don't open .ico files directly.

traits.compression: Each entry is PNG or uncompressed DIB
traits.colorDepth: 1 to 32 bits per pixel, per entry
traits.support: Windows, browsers (as favicons); few editors
traits.bestFor: Windows application icons and favicons

pdf.name: PDF
pdf.summary: PDF, introduced by Adobe in 1993 and standardised as ISO 32000, describes fixed-layout pages: text positioned with embedded fonts, vector drawings and images, so a document looks the same on every device and printer. That is why forms, invoices, contracts and scans travel as PDF. A PDF made from a scanner, however, often contains only a picture of each page with no real text layer.

traits.structure: Fixed-layout pages with text, vectors and images
traits.editability: Designed for viewing and printing, not editing
traits.support: Universal viewers in browsers and operating systems
traits.bestFor: Sharing, printing and submitting final documents

docx.name: DOCX
docx.summary: DOCX is the Office Open XML word-processing format introduced with Word 2007 and standardised as ECMA-376 / ISO/IEC 29500. A .docx file is a ZIP archive containing XML parts for the body text, styles, numbering, headers, footers, comments and embedded media. It is reflowable rather than fixed-layout, so the same document can look different in Word, Google Docs and LibreOffice.

traits.structure: ZIP of XML parts: paragraphs, runs, styles, tables, media
traits.support: Word, Google Docs, LibreOffice, Pages
traits.bestFor: Documents that are still being written or edited

csv.name: CSV
csv.summary: CSV stores a table as plain text: one record per line, fields separated by commas, and fields containing commas, quotes or line breaks wrapped in double quotes (with quotes doubled), as described in RFC 4180. It has no data types, no nesting and no declared encoding, and many European spreadsheet locales write semicolons instead of commas. It is still the lowest common denominator for exporting data from spreadsheets, databases and SaaS tools.

traits.support: Every spreadsheet, database and data tool
traits.bestFor: Moving tabular data between tools

tsv.name: TSV
tsv.summary: TSV is a table in plain text with a tab character between fields. Because tabs rarely occur inside real values, TSV usually needs no quoting at all, which makes it easy to process with command-line tools — and it is what spreadsheets put on the clipboard when you copy cells. The IANA definition does not allow tabs or line breaks inside fields, so values containing them must be quoted or escaped.

traits.support: Spreadsheets, Unix tools, bioinformatics and data warehouses
traits.bestFor: Clipboard exchange and command-line processing

json.name: JSON
json.summary: JSON (RFC 8259 / ECMA-404) represents data as nested objects and arrays of strings, numbers, booleans and null. It is the default format of web APIs, configuration files and NoSQL databases because every programming language can parse it. It has no comments, no date type and no schema built in, and numbers are only as precise as the parser reading them.

traits.support: Every programming language and web API
traits.bestFor: APIs, app data and configuration

xml.name: XML
xml.summary: XML, a W3C recommendation since 1998, marks data up with nested elements and attributes. It supports namespaces, schemas (XSD), comments and mixed text, which is why it underpins RSS feeds, SOAP services, sitemaps, SVG, Office documents and many enterprise and government data exchanges. It is verbose, and it distinguishes attributes from child elements — a distinction JSON, CSV and YAML don't have.

traits.structure: Tree of elements with attributes and text
traits.dataTypes: Text only, unless a schema says otherwise
traits.support: Enterprise systems, feeds, office formats, every language
traits.bestFor: Document-centric and schema-validated data exchange

yaml.name: YAML
yaml.summary: YAML expresses the same kind of data as JSON — mappings, sequences and scalars — using indentation instead of braces, and adds comments, multi-line strings, anchors/aliases and multiple documents per file. YAML 1.2 is a superset of JSON. It is the configuration language of Kubernetes, Docker Compose, GitHub Actions, Ansible and many static-site generators, where its readability matters more than parsing speed.

traits.structure: Tree of mappings and sequences, indentation-based
traits.support: DevOps tooling, CI systems and most languages via libraries
traits.bestFor: Human-edited configuration

xlsx.name: XLSX
xlsx.summary: XLSX is the Office Open XML spreadsheet format used by Excel since 2007: a ZIP archive of XML parts describing worksheets, shared strings, styles and more. Unlike CSV it stores cell types, multiple sheets, formatting, formulas and frozen panes. A worksheet holds at most 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns, and a cell at most 32,767 characters.

traits.structure: Workbook of typed worksheets (ZIP of XML)
traits.dataTypes: Numbers, text, booleans, dates (as serial numbers), formulas
traits.support: Excel, Google Sheets, LibreOffice Calc, Numbers
traits.bestFor: Spreadsheets people will open, filter and format

markdown.name: Markdown
markdown.summary: Markdown, created by John Gruber in 2004, is a plain-text syntax for formatting: # for headings, * or - for lists, **bold**, [links](url) and fenced code blocks. The original description was ambiguous, so CommonMark (2014) specified it precisely, and GitHub Flavored Markdown added tables, task lists, strikethrough and autolinks. README files, documentation sites, note apps and chat tools all use it.

traits.structure: Plain text with lightweight formatting marks
traits.support: GitHub, GitLab, documentation tools, note apps, chat apps
traits.bestFor: Writing formatted text that stays readable as plain text

html.name: HTML
html.summary:
HTML is the markup language of the web, maintained by WHATWG as a living standard. Elements such as

,

,

    , and describe the structure and meaning of content, while CSS and JavaScript add presentation and behaviour. HTML copied from web pages, CMS editors and email templates often carries inline styles, wrapper
    s and scripts on top of the actual content.

traits.support: Every browser, email client and CMS
traits.bestFor: Publishing documents on the web

txt.name: Text
txt.summary: Plain text is just characters and line breaks — no fonts, links, bold or layout. Today it is almost always UTF-8, which can represent every script and emoji. It is the most durable and searchable form of content, accepted by every editor, form field, command-line tool and language model.

traits.support: Universal
traits.bestFor: Searching, pasting, archiving and processing text

base64.name: Base64
base64.summary: Base64 (RFC 4648) represents arbitrary bytes using 64 safe ASCII characters (A–Z, a–z, 0–9, + and /), so binary data can travel through systems that only handle text: email attachments (MIME), data: URLs, JSON payloads, HTTP Basic auth headers and JWTs. Every 3 bytes become 4 characters, so encoded data is about 33% larger. Base64 is an encoding, not encryption — anyone can decode it.

traits.alphabet: A–Z a–z 0–9 + / with = padding (URL-safe variant uses - and _)
traits.bestFor: Embedding bytes in text-only channels

urlencoded.name: URL-encoded
urlencoded.summary: Percent-encoding, defined in RFC 3986, replaces characters that are not allowed or have special meaning in a URL with % followed by two hex digits of their UTF-8 bytes — a space becomes %20, é becomes %C3%A9. HTML form submissions use a close relative, application/x-www-form-urlencoded, where spaces become +. Getting the encoding wrong is a classic source of broken links, double-encoded %2520 sequences and query parameters that are cut off at an & sign.

traits.alphabet: Unreserved A–Z a–z 0–9 - . _ ~ kept; everything else as %XX
traits.sizeOverhead: Up to 3× for encoded bytes (9 characters for a 3-byte UTF-8 character)
traits.bestFor: Query strings, path segments and form bodies

srt.name: SRT
srt.summary: SRT comes from SubRip, a Windows tool that extracted subtitles from DVDs around 2000. Each cue is a counter, a time range written HH:MM:SS,mmm --> HH:MM:SS,mmm (note the comma before milliseconds), and one or more lines of text. It has no official specification and supports only basic tags like <i>, <b>, <u> and <font color>, but almost every video player, editor and platform imports it.

traits.support: Nearly every player, editor and video platform
traits.bestFor: Maximum compatibility

vtt.name: VTT
vtt.summary: WebVTT is the W3C caption format for HTML5 video: the <track> element only accepts WebVTT. A file must start with the line WEBVTT, timestamps use a dot before milliseconds (hours are optional), and cues can carry settings for position, line, size and alignment, voice spans (<v Speaker>), classes for CSS ::cue styling, NOTE comments and STYLE blocks.

traits.positioning: Cue settings: line, position, size, align, region
traits.support: Browsers (HTML5 <track>), web players, streaming platforms
traits.bestFor: Captions on web video

ass.name: ASS
ass.summary: Advanced SubStation Alpha (v4+) grew out of the SubStation Alpha editor and is today mostly written with Aegisub. An .ass file is an INI-like script with [Script Info], [V4+ Styles] and [Events] sections: named styles define fonts, colors, outlines and margins, and inline override tags such as {\pos(x,y)}, {\fad}, {\k} karaoke timing and {\an8} placement allow typesetting that plain SRT or VTT cannot express. Timestamps use centiseconds: H:MM:SS.cc.

traits.styling: Named styles plus override tags (fonts, colors, borders, effects)
traits.support: VLC, mpv, MPC-HC, Aegisub, fansub workflows; rarely web players
traits.bestFor: Styled, typeset or karaoke subtitles
